Orioles

Mailbag leftovers for breakfast

  • Roch Kubatko

  • November 24, 2026 4:00 am

  • 0 Comments

  • Share

Forget about Trevor Rogers coming back to the Orioles.

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:46
Instaread

Rogers and the Cubs reached agreement last night on a five-year contract, as first reported by MLB Network and confirmed by a source. The deal is worth $120 million and deferrals are included.

The $23.15 million qualifying offer was turned down, as expected, and the Orioles will receive a compensatory draft pick.

Rogers posted a 2.90 ERA in his last 20 starts after finishing 2025 with a 1.81 ERA in 18 starts and receiving a fifth-place vote in Cy Young balloting. He was the Orioles’ Opening Day starter this year.

They fixed him and they lost him.

Kyle Bradish, Shane Baz and Brandon Young are the top three pitchers in the rotation, and a left-hander could become more of a priority. Kris Bubic and Matthew Boyd are two of the available southpaws on their radar.

Let’s dig into some mailbag leftovers before raiding the fridge over the weekend for cold turkey and stuffing.

And speaking of stuffing, yes, it’s the best side dish besides mashed potatoes. I’ll die on that carb hill.

Cranberry sauce out of the can. Celery with cream cheese smeared on it. We’ve incorporated mac and cheese the past few years.

Does celery count as a green vegetable? Forget it. I’ll let you ask the questions.

Who is occupying the DH role to push Coby Mayo to the outfield?
Mayo’s a strong young man. It’s gonna take more than one person to push him. The DH spot is supposed to remain flexible and allow manager Craig Albernaz to rotate in players like Samuel Basallo, Christian Encarnacion-Strand, Jordan Westburg and Pete Alonso when he isn’t at first base. And these are just some of the names as the roster currently is constructed. More changes are on deck. It’s important to note that Mayo isn’t viewed as a possibility to hold down a full-time job in the outfield. If he’s shagging fly balls, it’s done to gauge his comfort level and whether he might be an option while the Orioles seek ways to keep his bat in the lineup. And hey, it also could increase his value if teams want to talk trade. Third base is crowded. Alonso has a stranglehold on first. Mayo’s got to play somewhere, and the Orioles need to figure it out, and that includes whether he’s going to get an opportunity to be more than a platoon guy.

Will Samuel Basallo get most of the starts behind the plate?
It’s an understandable assumption after the Orioles gave him an eight-year extension five days into his major league career and traded Adley Rutschman at the deadline. But Mike Elias has tamped down expectations of Basallo starting more than half the games. He’s going to get lots of reps at first base, where he’s made six starts. He received 99 plate appearances against left-handers this year and batted .172/.222/.237. More chances to catch obviously will come to him if the Orioles don’t restrict his usage to facing right-handers. And if the Orioles don’t sign or trade for a guy who’s better than a backup. Would Carlos Narváez make more starts than Basallo? I guess if Basallo becomes the popular choice to DH. But this isn’t how we envisioned Basallo’s career unfolding after the Orioles signed him for $1.3 million as part of the 2021 international class and he tore up minor league pitching and got paid by the new ownership group. His role is evolving.

Are the rumors that the O’s are talking to various players actually true, window dressing or just blatant lies?
Is it window dressing or stuffing? I’ll assume that you mean talking to agents who represent those players or teams that might be willing to trade them. Mike Elias is talking to a lot of people. He’s immersed in the trade and free agent markets. I guess this is the yearly reminder that a lack of news shouldn’t be mistaken for a lack of activity. It takes two to make a deal. But no one is lying about negotiations. Meanwhile, since I brought it up, dressing is baked outside the bird and stuffing is cooked inside of it.

Do you agree that it’s impossible to put too much gravy on a Thanksgiving dinner?
No. It’s too much if the meal is served in a bowl to reduce spillage. But leftover white meat can get drier than kindling. Soak it and save yourselves. I truly believe that most 911 calls over the holidays are due to the choking hazard from turkey breasts. My mom is a wonderful cook, but she swears that the pop-up timer is just a suggestion. Check back in an hour or so. You’d think that she lived through the salmonella typhi scare during the Spanish-American War.

If the team doesn’t bring back Trevor Rogers, who are the candidates in free agency that are the best fits to fill out the rotation?
This question obviously was submitted before last night, and these are two categories. A staff ace and a veteran for the back end. Rogers is a top-of-the-rotation guy and the Orioles need to aim high for his replacement. It would have been easier to just re-sign him, but we always double back to the question of how much they’re willing to spend on pitching. And with Tarik Skubal off the board, more teams were going to pivot to Rogers. He might have celebrated that contract almost as hard as Skubal. Freddy Peralta seemed unlikely, but the sides reportedly have held discussions. Michael King can be an ace if he stays healthy and he’s more affordable. Sonny Gray is off the board. Now we’re down to next-tier starters like Nick Martinez, Clay Holmes, Tyler Mahle, Matthew Boyd, Kris Bubic and Foster Griffin.

We hear a lot of excuses for the Orioles’ failures, but why is no one asking the matter of fact question of why teams like the Guardians, Brewers and Rays always draft low but develop players consistently, yet the Orioles failed on so many high draft picks?
No one is asking about the struggles to develop young talent? I feel like it’s a popular topic, why highly rated prospects level out or regress. Mike Elias and general manager Jared Banner have addressed it. Banner reminds us that he’s new here and still learning the roster. His player development background was a big reason why the Orioles pursued him. Mike Shildt is in the organization to assist in this area. Cal Ripken Jr. is keying on fundamentals. Your question is a fair one, and it’s asked. I bet a Google search will uncover some of the responses.

If you had to pick a last meal (not dying or anything, just lost a bet) what would you want?
Dry white meat and a bucket of gravy. Oh, you’re serious. Thanks for not assuming that my last meal is tied to a crime that I committed. A medium-rare steak – New York strip or porterhouse preferred – my mom’s sour cream mashed potatoes, corn to mix into the potatoes, and a Manhattan with a big cube or a Tito’s dirty martini. I’ll also take Crystal Head vodka if it’s available, but that’s a hard find.

Do the Orioles need a closer?
They already have two. Does the team with the most closers on the roster earn a Wild Card? Maybe that will be part of the new CBA. It wouldn’t hurt to have a set-up guy with some closing experience besides Yennier Cano, who’s more effective before the ninth inning. Andrew Kittredge is a free agent, but he’s an example.
